value: in vitro, whole etiolated sporophytes produced the most new sporophytes per initial sporophyte under blue LED light (315.2), 2.7, 9 and 18.2 times the numbers under fluorescent, red-blue and red light; fresh weight under blue did not differ from fluorescent (1.1 g vs 1.62 g)
method: in vitro culture of whole sporophytes under monochromatic or mixed LED spectra versus fluorescent control, number of newly formed sporophytes per initial sporophyte counted after 6 months
conditions: In vitro culture on hormone-free half-strength MS medium (0.7% plant agar, pH 5.8; 2% sucrose for whole sporophytes); whole etiolated 5-month-old sporophytes with 3-4 leaves, six jars of four initial sporophytes per light quality, read after 6 months; LEDs B (100% blue, 430 nm), R (100% red, 670 nm), RB (70% red, 30% blue; no separate wavelengths given), all at PPFD 40 umol m-2 s-1 (LI-250A meter, BTS256 spectrometer); control Fl = fluorescent Philips TL-D 36W/54 lamps (not LED). Contrary and null results from the same paper: fresh weight of plants under control Fl (1.62 g) and B (1.1 g) did not differ statistically after 6 months; B, R and RB did not affect leaf development compared with fluorescent light (Figure 4B); in the separate stipe-explant experiment (2.5 mm explants from etiolated sporophytes, 3 dishes x 20 explants per light) the best light was RBY (35% red, 15% blue, 50% yellow 600 nm; 20.6 sporophytes at 3D/5L), not blue. Caveats: the 315.2 value has no SD or letters in the text (Figure 4 uses a Dunn-Bonferroni test at p <= 0.05; the letters were not in the text I read, so which comparisons were significant is not confirmed); one species, one in vitro culture system, one intensity. This is a tissue-culture multiplication response: new sporophytes formed on cultured sporophytes, a response of the living culture to light quality, not a field or whole-plant-in-soil result.

value: in vitro, a, b and total chlorophyll (ug per g fresh weight) in Cyathea delgadii sporophytes was greatest under blue (B) and red-blue (RB) LED spectra; red light alone was ineffective for pigment accumulation
method: in vitro culture of whole sporophytes under LED spectra versus fluorescent control, photosynthetic pigments extracted and measured after culture; reported per g fresh weight (Figure 5)
conditions: In vitro culture on hormone-free half-strength MS medium (0.7% plant agar, pH 5.8; 2% sucrose for whole sporophytes); whole etiolated 5-month-old sporophytes with 3-4 leaves, six jars of four initial sporophytes per light quality, read after 6 months; LEDs B (100% blue, 430 nm), R (100% red, 670 nm), RB (70% red, 30% blue; no separate wavelengths given), all at PPFD 40 umol m-2 s-1 (LI-250A meter, BTS256 spectrometer); control Fl = fluorescent Philips TL-D 36W/54 lamps (not LED). Contrary and related results from the same paper: the paper says R light alone was ineffective for accumulation of all photosynthetic pigments studied (Section 3.4) and carotenoids were lower than total chlorophyll under every light, greatest under B (2.39 ug g-1 fresh weight); the abstract says RB and B stimulated chlorophyll accumulation better than Fl. The text gives no chlorophyll numbers (Figure 5 only, not read); pigment replicates are printed 'Tree biological replicates' (probably three). Other results: fresh weight of plants under control Fl (1.62 g) and B (1.1 g) did not differ statistically after 6 months; B, R and RB did not affect leaf development compared with fluorescent light (Figure 4B); in the separate stipe-explant experiment (2.5 mm explants from etiolated sporophytes, 3 dishes x 20 explants per light) the best light was RBY (35% red, 15% blue, 50% yellow 600 nm; 20.6 sporophytes at 3D/5L), not blue. Caveats: the 315.2 value has no SD or letters in the text (Figure 4 uses a Dunn-Bonferroni test at p <= 0.05; the letters were not in the text I read, so which comparisons were significant is not confirmed); one species, one in vitro culture system, one intensity. This is a tissue-culture multiplication response: a response of the living culture to light quality, not a field or whole-plant-in-soil result. Chlorophyll content is a physiological response to light quality, not a yield measure.
